speechtext:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROPOSED LEGISLATION BY ONTARIO IN FIELD OF BANKING

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce may I direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister with reference to the proposed Caribbean conference which is to be held at Saint Lucia shortly. Are any discussions to take place at that conference with respect to an international agreement on the price of sugar?

Inquiries of the Ministry
The Prime Minister will remember that a year or two ago when I suggested we should follow the example of the United States and Great Britain in getting a guaranteed price range for sugar which would provide some price stability to the Canadian consumer, the former minister of trade and commerce suggested that the world price was too high. It is now the lowest it has been for several decades. Is the government pursuing the question of an international agreement for sugar, and will such a policy be discussed at this forthcoming conference?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, we are actively pursuing the idea of an international sugar agreement, which I think is the best way of dealing with the problem and helping our friends in the Caribbean at the same time. But in the absence of a program along those lines we will be discussing with the governments at the conference, which is to be held on the official level, other ways in which we might possibly be able to assist the sugar producers of that part of the world pending the working out of an international trade agreement.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister whether any discussions have been held with the government of Jamaica, and what progress has been made if such discussions have been held.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISCUSSIONS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister whether, in view of the initiative taken by the premier of Ontario in connection with an over-all study of confederation and the constitution and his invitation to other governments to meet with him, and in view of the initiative previously taken by at least one other province in this regard, he
January 27, 1967

will urgently consider accelerating the federal government's study of this matter? The objective would be of course to enable a parliamentary committee to be established at an early date so that parliament could give consideration to this matter so as to insure in turn that the federal government is not caught short when the provinces have com-leted their studies.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we expect to have our studies completed in time for any constitutional conference which could usefully be called after all the preparatory work has been done at the federal and provincial levels. As soon as the federal study has been completed by the government this matter will be submitted to a parliamentary committee.
I should point out that the statement of the premier of Ontario on this question did not visualize a constitutional conference, but rather a meeting the nature of which is not clear in my mind, but at which the constitution as it is at present would be discussed. I hope shortly to be in touch with the premier of Ontario by correspondence to find out what he had in mind when he made his announcement.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister indicate to the house in general terms his projected timetable in respect of this study? When might we expect a committee of this parliament to be established to study this question under the proposed timetable?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I do not think it would be possible to do that until the autumn at the earliest.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister reconsider that timetable in order that we will not be in the position of not having completed our study when the provinces come forward with a formal position? subtopic: REQUEST FOR ACCELERATED STUDY BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT

I do not think the provinces will have completed their study before the federal government and this parliament have considered the matter. However, that will be a matter for them to decide. I know that in construing a statute one can pay little attention to what goes on in the legislature where it was enacted. But 1 would still hope that notwithstanding the fact that there may be that imperfection, the commission would never make any determination under that clause and under one or two others without having public hearings. I feel that is very important, and that all interested parties should be permitted to attend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to join with the Minister of Transport in emphasizing as well as I can that when parliament does do a good job, as it has done with this transportation bill, the country should know about it. I think during this session in the handling of the medicare discussion, in the handling of the guaranteed income supplement proposal, and particularly in the handling of this transportation bill, we on both sides of the house have demonstrated to the whole country that when parliament puts its mind to it it can do a good job.
I have had something to do with railway legislation such as that which is now before
[Mr. Bell (Carleton) .1
us for a good many years, Mr. Speaker. When the royal commission report was submitted to the previous government in 1962 it was our task to make the first drafts of a transportation bill. At that time the bill dealt primarily with railways. It was our concern then how we could manage the railways more efficiently and yet allow for the maximum of freedom.
So far as the rationalization concept was concerned, we felt at that time that this should be kept within the power of the elected representatives of the people in the central government of Canada and that we should deal directly and co-operatively with those provinces that do have rationalization problems. To that end, Mr. Speaker, an informal agreement was reached with the provincial premiers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as to the course we would follow in the procedure of rationalization.
It is on this question, Mr. Speaker, that I still have some lingering doubts about this bill, but I have said enough already in this house to indicate what those doubts are. Therefore, in summarizing the first part of my remarks I should like to say that this parliament has demonstrated that it can take a very involved bill, affecting a large section of the economy of this country, and draft legislation which admittedly is venturing into an unknown field in turning over vast delegated powers to a board on a problem we know very little about. In this respect we have made a good effort to produce a bill that will give some guide lines to this new board.
Using round figures, Mr. Speaker, over 40 amendments were proposed to the draft of the bill as submitted to the standing committee in 1966. In the committee in this chamber approximately a further score were added, and some were turned down. I think this is reason for complimenting the government for being flexible, on the one hand, and above all for pointing out that for the most part the opposition has been constructive and has tried to be helpful to the government in producing a better bill.
There is one matter, Mr. Speaker, about which I still wish to place a caveat on the record. As I mentioned a few moments ago, the government to which I belonged intended to carry out the rationalization provisions of the proposed operation of the railways in Canada through the co-operative efforts of the provincial governments and the federal government.
January 27, 1967

In the bill as it is now a new principle has been brought in which turns the powers of the elected representatives over to a delegated board which is to carry out these rationalization provisions. On behalf of our party I stated on second reading and in committee that we reluctantly accepted this principle in an effort to try to achieve the efficiency in the management of our transportation system that a modem economy required.
In our amendments we tried to do two things under the general principles about which I am talking. On the one hand we tried to strengthen the hand of the board in order that it could better do its job. Simultaneously we tried to keep in the hands of the elected representatives-in other words in parliament, the House of Commons and the Senate-a little more control over this board to which we delegated such vast powers.
The caveat I want to register, Mr. Speaker, is that I still feel it would not have done any harm and would have strengthened the bill considerably had we given that board the power to direct as well as to recommend. In view of the pressure of the subsidies, we could have given to that board considerable authority to express to railway management that where there were ways to run the railways better and save money and thereby keep tariffs down, and perhaps the board could have got its way more effectively with the railways had it been given power to direct. We lost that amendment, Mr. Speaker, but we make no apologies for having made the try.
Simultaneously with trying to strengthen the power of the board to do its job properly the hon. member for Peace River also moved an amendment to set up a more sophisticated means by which parliament could control one of its agencies, whether it be a crown corporation or a board. This proposal too was voted down in committee. I think that was a mistake, and I hope it does not turn out to be fatal. I know that in theory the standing committee on transportation has the right to examine the workings of this board. I also know that because of the lack of skilled professional help at the command of the standing committee there is not a great deal that laymen can do.
[DOT] (12 noon)
For two or three years after passage of this bill, because of the interest aroused in its preparation over the last few years, a number of members will take an active interest in this
Transportation
matter and maintain their knowledge. Ultimately, from apathy, from human nature, the interest will drop, and I am afraid the board will have tremendous powers without full and proper control by parliament. Nobody will be interested enough to look at it, to exercise the control that is needed.
If a government wants to play games it is possible, under the rules of the house, to delay the setting up of a committee until far into the session. At that time other things occupy hon. members and little may be done. We should prefer that a standing committee be set up in such a way that the government could not interfere with the way the board is brought under review. We should like to have that committee under the chairmanship of an opposition member. We started that principle in the public accounts committee some eight years ago and it has worked very well. I think it would work just as well here.
Third, we should like to see that committee buttressed by at least three highly qualified individuals able to deal with technical matters that the ordinary layman member of the house cannot deal with, in order that the chairman of the committee and the committee may be aware of what is happening on the board. It is in this area that trouble will arise. The interest of the House of Commons will not be maintained, and as a result I can see the board becoming a power unto itself. There will be no machinery or capacity to check and control it, unless there is a serious uproar here, in the house.
All this was dealt with in committee. I do not have to rehash it. I have made my point. This party is concerned about our handing over tremendous powers to this board without there being more sophisticated means to strengthen our committee to control that body.
Another point I want to raise in summary has to do with the Crowsnest pass rates. This matter is always dealt with emotionally because for over half a century thousands of Canadians have depended on this rate structure to operate their industries and make a living. It has not been repeated often enough in this debate that at the beginning a contract was made. That contract has been modified over the years, but its essence was that if a group of men built a railway, certain things would be done. The railway, the Canadian Pacific, received tremendous land acreages, valuable oil and mineral rights, forest lands,
*

huge sums of money and monopolies in certain areas. In return it was to carry our grain seaward at a fixed rate.
With advances in automation and engineering, instead of an engineer and crew operating a train of 25 box cars they now can operate a train with 100 box cars. The sooner the railways realize there is modern equipment, the better. Modern, enlarged cars are available, with improved techniques of grain handling in the prairie areas and terminals the cost will be kept constant. Change will keep it constant. The railways cannot argue they are losing money on the Crowsnest pass rates. They have used this argument as a constant propaganda pressure on the people of western Canada. They have tried to maintain the myth that they lose money on these rates, but the truth is that they do not lose money.
The 1964 bill introduced by the government said that if there were losses under the Crowsnest Pass rates there would be a charge on the treasury. In this bill, the 1966 bill, that section has been taken out. When I raised this matter on second reading the minister said the section was taken out because there are no losses on the Crowsnest Pass rates; yet the section having to do with the review was included. My colleague for Winnipeg South Centre moved an amendment to that, and the majority of this parliament spoke with him. Owing to the tradition that Mr. Speaker always maintains the rules, the parliamentary wish prevailed, and I hope that matter is dead, dead, dead.
The pact was made. The railways got their part of the contract; they shall honour their obligation under the contract. The other day, looking at evidence showing the peripheral advantages the railways got as part of the agreement, I saw that one of them was rights to minerals. One peripheral operation alone has assets today of approximately $400 million. I will not mention the value of oil and gas rights which will increase as the years go by and as discoveries continue. I do not mention the value of the tremendous forest tracts the railways have and still enjoy. I could list all the things the railway got, and I have little use for those who say that because the railways got all the cream and they are down to the skimmed milk, we should make a new contract.
The Crowsnest pass rates are a part of our national structure, and I hope discussion of them is over. Parliament has spoken. The bill will get through. I hope nobody raises this
	j
issue again. The people of western Canada thank opposition members of parliament for the amendment which was carried.
On the question of maximum rate control and costing we are moving into the unknown. I can only say that the best chance all Canadians will have is if we give the board the power to obtain competent personnel to deal with costing and work out a system of accounting, that we may know what things cost, and that we need not accept the figures of the railways. If this could be done, if competent staff could be selected by the board, many of us would feel relief. We know we are not competent to deal with these questions. Few people in Canada are competent to deal with costing and maximum rate control matters. It is in the field of freight rates that the battle can be lost. I hope the board gets people competent to deal with these matters, that we may feel protected.
I will not talk about the public interest, the general public vis-a-vis the shipper. That has been adequately covered in previous discussions. This matter concerns quite a few people. We shall see what will happen.
Finally, the government will be responsible for the selection of the personnel of this board. I need not warn the minister-rightly or wrongly, I hate to lay the blame on an individual-but the attitude of the Canadian public toward the Board of Transport Commissioners is not good. We feel, whether by its rules and regulations, the precedents it follows and so on, it has always accepted the railway position. In selecting this new board dealing with railways, air, water, buses, trucks, and pipe lines the government will be on the spot to produce the type of commissioner, at the top, in whom the people of Canada can have confidence. We hope that in the next few years a staff will be collected around this individual capable of coping as an equal with the giants of the transportation industry. This is an old, old sore on the social hide of the Canadian people.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Here is an opportunity for the minister and his colleagues to realize that they have had a good run for their money in the house with regard to this bill. We have fought the hon. gentleman where we thought we should fight; we have been constructive where we thought we should be constructive. We have tried to help the minister. Now will he help us and the Canadian people by giving us a board which will address itself effectively and with sincerity to the task before it, and act as a
January 27, 1967

reliable referee between the general public and the transportation companies?
We can only hope that if we get such a board the railways will be able to function efficiently, the air lines will be able to give full service to the public, and all the other dorms of transportation will be able to operate in an effective way for the betterment of this country. Certainly the principle of integrating all transport service is a new one for us in Canada. It seems logical, and in the light of the arguments which have been advanced we have agreed to delegate this power to a commission. Now we have done so it is up to the government to produce the type of board having the competence needed to make this bill a lasting success.

During the time this bill was before the committee of the whole house I personally did not become too involved in it. I think hon. members will agree that I did not take up the time of the committee for very long. However, at this point I should like to make a few comments on the measure.
I should like to say at the outset, as far as the general concept of the bill is concerned, that the members of my party, together, I think, with hon. members in other parties, are agreed that the time for setting up a commission which would have jurisdiction over all modes of transport was long overdue. In my opinion this is the most important factor in a good gransport policy for a country such as ours. But the minister will have to watch these matters very carefully in order to make sure the commission is applying itself properly to its primary purpose, the co-ordination of all the different modes of transport in such a manner that they will work in conjunction with one another rather than against one another as happens now, in so many cases, to the disadvantage of the general public.
I was a member of the standing committee on transport and communications, and I will say at once that I commend the chairman of that committee for the excellent work he did. I do not think it would be right if I neglected to say, too, that the minister himself has been very helpful all along. At times he seemed to bend over backward in order to get along not only with the standing committee but the committee of the whole house. I might also say a word of commendation to my hon. friend from Springfield who carried the ball for our party on this issue, for the contribution he made to our discussions. All hon.
Transportation
members will agree, I believe, that he is to be commended on the way he carried out this task, and that while doing so he offered a number of very worth-while suggestions.
It is not my intention to discuss the bill at great length. During the committee stage I indicated that in my view there was a deficiency in the legislation. I still believe this deficiency exists. It has to do with the consequences of the abandonment of branch lines. The amendment I moved in committee would have provided some relief for employees adversely affected by rail line abandonment to the extent that they were required to relocate or, in extreme cases, lost their jobs altogether. It was a matter of great regret to me that this amendment failed to secure acceptance.
I have an amendment here-I do not think I need go into it too deeply-which expresses what I have said previously on this subject, and I intend to move it now, seconded by my hon. friend from York South. I have a limited number of copies in English and in French for distribution. It reads as follows:
That Bill C-231 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for reconsideration of clause 42 in relation to the matter of compensation to employees adversely affected by railway abandonment or rationalization.

I wonder whether before the motion is put to the house it would be too hazardous for me to raise a point of order. I do not wish to take any unnecessary time in arguing the point of order, because it would appear to me that this amendment is in substance the same as an amendment which was moved in committee of the whole, at which time it was ruled out of order by the chairman on the ground that it was beyond the scope of the bill, inasmuch as the bill does not deal with labour relations or industrial relations.
My position, substantially, is that the judgment made in the committee on this matter was sound. The bill in no way deals with any aspect of the relationship between the employees of any carriers and the carriers themselves. It seeks to lay down broad policies with respect to the relationship between the government and transport companies, between shippers and transport companies, but it does not in any way enter into the field of labour relations. I submit it would be wrong to attempt to direct the committee to do something which the chairman of that committee ruled as being outside the competence of that committee. To do so would, I suggest

Mr. Speaker, like the Minister of Transport I shall be brief because we have spent quite some time on procedural matters this week, but it does seem to me that this amendment is within the four corners of the kind of amendments that are in order on third reading. Citation 415 on page 287 of Beauchesne's fourth edition states:
When a bill comes up for third reading a member may move that it be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in any particular.
There are a number of other citations which spell out that point. The minister does not quarrel with that, but he contends that the amendment is beyond the scope of the bill because it deals with something which the bill does not include.
I remind Your Honour of the earlier discussion we had in committee of the whole on this matter. I think the situation was different, but some of the points that were made then apply now. I also remind Your Honour that clause 42 of the bill has a subheading which reads "Abandonment and Rationalization of Lines or Operations." In other words, the subject of abandonment and rationalization is in the bill. I also remind Your Honour that the resolution preceding the bill, as recorded at page 7743 of Hansard for August 29, 1966, listed many things that the bill would do and concluded with this phrase:
-and to provide further for other matters consequential upon or related or incidental to any of the foregoing.
I submit that if abandonment and rationalization of railway lines is one of the subjects of the bill, and if one of the purposes of the bill is to provide for matters consequential upon or related or incidental to any of the matters in the bill, then surely it is appropriate to ask for consideration of the consequences to employees of abandonment or rationalization of railway lines.
When we were in committee of the whole one of the arguments advanced was that the kind of amendment which my colleague moved at that stage might involve the expenditure of money out of the treasury, and thus it was not open to a private member to move it. We are not now at that stage. We are at

third reading, where it is possible to move that the bill be referred back for consideration of a matter, it being recognized that such a motion, even if it passes, is not compulsory and therefore does not run up against the problem of finance so far as a private member is concerned.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, there are many precedents for this and there is much that could be said, but I do not think we want to go into it at length today. My notes, which I have looked at quickly in order to refresh my memory, tell me that on the Canada Pension Plan legislation we were allowed to refer it back on such matters as the amount of the old age pension and the age at which it would be paid. Likewise we were allowed to refer the medicare bill back to the committee of the whole for reconsideration of the effective date and one or two other matters.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the kind of amendment now proposed by my colleague is similar to those amendments and that Your Honour should, and I trust will, find it to be in order.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to address myself briefly to the point of order. I would point out that in citation 415 in Beauchesne's fourth edition there is also subparagraph (4) which reads as follows:
On the third reading of a bill, an amendment to refer back to the committee of the whole must not tend to change the principle approved on the second reading.
When one relates this citation and its principle to the argument adduced by the Minister of Transport, it is our submission that the amendment goes beyond the principle of the bill which has to do with rates, tariffs, and regulation. The amendment deals with a subject which is foreign to the substance of the bill in that it refers to the relationship between the railways as employers and the employees, a matter involving negotiation, conciliation and other matters falling within the ambit of a labour bill.
I do not argue for a moment that the substance of what the amendment proposes is not important and will some day, and some day soon, have to be brought before this house, but what I do adduce by way of submission to Your Honour is that it is foreign to the principle of this bill and therefore inadmissible under citation 415(4) of Beauchesne, and is irrelevant because it does not deal with the main purport of the bill.

The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Fawcett), seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) moves:
That Bill C-231 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for reconsideration of clause 42 in relation to the matter of compensation to employees adversely affected by railway abandonment or rationalization.
The Minister of Transport has taken exception to this amendment on a point of order which has been supported by the Minister without Portfolio. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre bases his argument in support of the validity of the motion on citation 415 (1) of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which states:
When a bill comes up for third reading a member may move that it be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it in any particular.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre claims that the use of these words "in any particular" supports his contention that this amendment should be accepted. I cannot agree with him in spite of the fact that Beauchesne reads as has been indicated by the hon. member. Obviously there must be limitations on the type of amendments that can be moved on third reading. For example, the proposed amendment must be relevant to the bill which it seeks to amend; it should not seek to give a mandatory instruction to the committee, and it should not contradict the principle of the bill adopted on second reading. I point out these last two as examples of what these amendments should not do.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has restated the argument which had been made in committee to the effect that the subject matter which the hon. member for Nickel Belt would want the committee to reconsider is within the scope of the bill. I remind him that there has already been a

judgment of the Chair in committee to the effect that this proposal is outside the scope of the bill. The hon. member is now trying to do indirectly what could not be done in committee in view of the decision of the Chair.
A decision was reached that this proposition is outside the scope of the bill, and for this reason I cannot see how the house can direct the committee to consider an aspect of the matter which has already been ruled out of order by way of decision of the chairman of committees. Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a very brief comment on third reading of the bill which is before us. I appreciate, of course, that the amendment is not before the house, but I do wish to indicate that there are in this bill some very serious omissions.
As I understand the bill it is the hope of the government, and certainly the hope of the railways, that when it becomes law the railways will have more revenue. The question is, where is that addition to their revenue to come from? A great deal has been made of the suggestion during this debate, particularly by the minister-and I also have seen statements by officers of the railways to the same effect-that the railways will obtain more revenue as a result of increased competition between various modes of transport. I have very grave doubt as to whether that will result in any very large increase in railway income. I have very grave doubt whether there are sufficient areas where there will be genuine competition between the modes of transport and where the railways really will be able to benefit from the alleged increase in competition.
Time, of course, will prove whether one is right, but as I see the bill as a whole its real object is to provide the railways with added revenues by virtue of (a) abandonment of lines, (b) rationalization of lines and operations and, (c) payments from the treasury, some on a temporary basis and some on a permanent basis to recompense the railways for any losses they may have as a result of rationalization or as a result of other things which the bill covers. I submit that a realistic view of this bill will show not that the railways will receive more money as a result of the alleged increase in competition, but that they no doubt will make a killing out of the

January 27, 1967
Transportation
three areas I have suggested-abandonment, rationalization and the federal treasury.
I do not at all agree that it is a good thing for Canada to have a transportation policy which reduces the extent of regulation of the rates, tariffs and operations of the carriers. I do not at all agree that it is possible in a modern economy and in a modern society to permit transportation operations to be carried on more by the laws of the jungle rather than less. This, however, is what the minister wants to do, and in doing it he takes the greatest possible care, in every part of the bill, to make certain that as a result of his law the carriers will not suffer. In situations where they suffer losses as a result of carrying grain or other products because public policy demands it, or in situations where they refrain from abandonment because the commission might think it is not in the public interest, the federal treasury may be dipped into. I do not say it will be in all cases. This is a matter of argument. It will be a matter of judgment and discretion; but in every case where the result of the bill may be a loss to the railways, the minister has provided compensation for them.
The bill, however, contains not a word about compensation for the workers who may be adversely affected by rationalization or abandonment. It contains not a word about compensation to the communities which may be literally obliterated by the railways as a result of rationalization or abandonment of lines. It provides not a word about compensation for the shippers, and particularly the farmers who undoubtedly will suffer a very considerable loss in many cases as a result either of abandonment or rationalization. It seems to me that this is as one sided a piece of legislation as could be conceived in the ambit of transportation. It is almost deserving of the term class legislation. At every stage of the bill and on two separate occasions the minister sought to make sure that the companies will not only be compensated in some areas which possibly could be understood, but also, if it could be shown that they have suffered losses through the statutory rates as a result of the application of public policy, inquiries will be held.
While the amendment which the minister finally did get accepted by the Chair and by the committee of the whole house did not give the minister precise permission to establish an inquiry and did not give the railways the precise opportunity to request such an inquiry, nevertheless it did adopt, as the minister

said, a suggestion of mine that the commission already had that power under clause 15. Obviously it is the intention of the minister to have an inquiry into the Crowsnest pass rates to find out whether the railways are suffering losses as a result of them and to have a recommendation from the commission which would cause the governor in council to consider compensation. That is what the amendment which is now in the bill clearly implies, even though it implies it in a roundabout way by saying that the compensation will not be paid if the railways have increased certain rates. This exception underlines the intent that where the exception does not exist they will be paid compensation. So at every stage in the bill they have made provision for this.
The minister was accused by some hon. members of having made an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway that these things would be in the bill. The minister denied this and, of course, I accept his word without hesitation or reservation. But, none the less, I have no doubt that the minister has bought lock, stock and barrel the argument of the Canadian Pacific Railway with regard to the right policies. I accept his word that he has not made any agreement with them, but he has accepted their philosophy; he has accepted their theory of the right kind of transportation policy.

speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to say that I did accept the views of a most distinguished Canadian who recently died-one of the most respected residents of western Canada-and his fellow commissioners. Mr. Speaker, the late Mr. M. A. MacPherson was not a member of parliament and obviously is unable to say whether he should take responsibility for the minister's bill. I respectfully suggest to the minister that he cannot escape his responsibility by what he has just said. I repeat that by the terms of his bill it is obvious that the minister has accepted the philosophy of the C.P.R. concerning what the transportation policy should be.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Over the years when I have served on conciliation boards and in arbitration proceedings I have heard spokesmen for the C.P.R. state all the philosophies embodied in
January 27, 1967

this bill. They have said "We have always been under strict regulation to which the bus, ship and air line companies are not subject. Give us more competition with them and we will do something for you." They always say "We lose hundreds of millions of dollars over the years because of the uneconomic passenger service we must provide under public policy. Do something about that; let us rationalize and abandon branch lines and we will then be healthy."
This has been what officials of the poor, poverty stricken, penniless C.P.R. have told us. They have always claimed that the C.P.R. loses hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of the Crowsnest pass rates, and have always said to us serving on various boards that this is why they cannot pay their workers decent wages. They have said they would be glad to do so because they are as interested in their welfare as we are. They say "We weep for the fact that the railway workers have lost their position in the labour force in Canada", and they say they are as deeply concerned and weep as copiously about this as anyone else.
Having said all that, the officials then ask us to give them back the hundreds of millions of dollars they have lost because of the Crowsnest pass rates and because of the uneconomical passenger service and they will do justice to their employees. I have heard these officials say this since 1952 when I first had something to do with these conciliation boards.
The minister has embodied provisions in this bill in respect of every one of their claims, without exception. He has made certain that when this poverty stricken C.P.R. suffers a loss as a result of public policy, or can show such a loss by using the kind of cost accounting it indulges in, the people of Canada will compensate it from the federal treasury. I have never been able to accept that position, and I have said in reports to which 1 have been a party, and in some which I wrote and signed in person, that I could not accept the proposition that the C.P.R. is separate as to its rail operations from the rest of its activities.
As a citizen of Canada and as a member of this parliament I cannot accept the idea that there is something sacred in respect of the total empire of the C.P.R. with which rail operations must not be associated. As has been said time and time again, the C.P.R. came into existence historically as a result of tremendous financial and land grants from 23033-781

the people of Canada. Those grants enabled the C.P.R. to become established, and it was the revenues from rail operations and those grants that enabled the C.P.R. to acquire an air line, a huge mining and smelting company, oil operations and a tremendous amount of industrial and financial activity which now makes the C.P.R. one of the largest and richest corporations in this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: What a shame.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: I think it is a shame to exploit the Canadian people for that purpose. I am only concerned at this point, however, with the false proposition that it is fair, reasonable and just to compensate the C.P.R. for its losses in rail operations without taking into account any of its profits from the rest of its operations because that is taboo. When one deals with labour relations and employees of the C.P.R. he is limited to a consideration of the revenues and costs relating only to its rail operations. One must not look at the economy of the company as a whole but must only look at its rail operations.

Yes; as my leader says, when the C.P.R. asks the Board of Transport Commissioners to increase its rates that board is limited to a consideration of their cost accounting and their figures in relation to rail operations, and must not consider or take into account other revenue. I don't agree with this.
At one point during the debate in committee of the whole house-and he will correct me if I am wrong or misrepresenting him-the minister said the government had made a definite decision not to include in this bill anything in respect of the labour relations of the railway companies. 1 am sure I remember that correctly. The minister admits that he made a definite decision to compensate the railway companies for their losses but to do nothing about the losses which the employees of the railways companies will suffer as a result of the implementation of this bill, and nothing about the losses to the communities and farmers which will result from its implementation.
I hope for the sake of Canada that the minister will be proved right in his feeling that there will be added competition which will benefit the society and economy of Canada, and that I am wrong in my conviction, on the basis of my understanding of

Canada's transportation system, that this attempt to reintroduce the law of the jungle in the transportation world, to reduce the amount of regulation and to encourage the railways to dip further into the treasury, will not serve the transportation economy of this country well.
It is my feeling that all this will present us in years to come with precisely the same claims, complaints, difficulties and injustices that this parliament has heard about transportation policy for many decades. It is my view that there have been serious oversights in the minister's consideration of this problem. Perhaps when I say "oversights" I am being too kind. The minister has drafted a bill on principles which are outdated. He has been far too lenient and soft so far as the railway companies in Canada are concerned, particularly the C.P.R. On the other hand, the minister has been far too cavalier about the real problems facing the communities, the workers of the railway companies, and the farmers in Canada who will be adversely affected by the provisions of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to speak at any length, but I do want to say a few words at this stage. We have been considering this bill of great magnitude, and we all know about the years of work and effort of royal commissions, committee members, various ministers and government officials which was undertaken to produce this bill. It is one of the most important and copious bills ever to be dealt with or considered by this house, but I do not believe for one moment that it will cure all the ills of the transportation systems in Canada.
Problems in relation to transportation are going to stay with us for the next hundred years, just as they have been with us for the past hundred years. People will continue to refer to one place in this house as the railway committee room, or perhaps that name will be changed to the transportation committee room. That is a clear indication of the tremendous interest of the parliament and people of Canada in this subject.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
This is an attempt to solve some of the problems, but I expect that year after year problems of transportation will be raised in this chamber. I expect there will be amendments to this bill year after year, that there will be further committee study and that people will be wrestling with this problem, no

matter how young they may be or how many new ideas they may have with regard to how things should be run in Canada. This is a problem that has confronted us for a hundred years, and it will continue. Whether the minister and the government have made an advance on the present situation only time will tell. I am not convinced that the solution presented to us in the bill is necessarily the best one. It will now have to be given a trial, because the house has reached the point where it is approving the bill.
I do not like the idea of the large commission and the czar who will preside over it. I do not know who that will be, but I just do not like the general idea. I think ministerial responsibility has been decreased by this creation; parliamentary control has been diminished. It has been bad enough in the past asking questions of the Minister of Transport, who says "Well, I will convey your question to the management of the C.N.R. and see what sort of answer I get." We will now be even further removed from control over transportation. So I am not very impressed and am not too hopeful that anything spectacular has been achieved. I recognize that freight rates will rise. I think it is safe to predict that the people in the Atlantic provinces and the western provinces of Canada will be paying more for transportation services. I think there is an element of inflation involved here.
As a resident of western Canada I cannot really rejoice in what has been done. I think there will be a continuation in the future of subsidization by the government. That is the history of transportation in this country. I doubt very much that the subsidization factor has been removed. It is faint praise that I have for the bill. It is faint praise that I have for the government for the way it organized the business of the house in regard to this bill. The minister was eager and anxious to get it completed last fall. He introduced it at the time of the special session when we were called back here to discuss an entirely different matter. He urged us repeatedy in the day and a half just before Christmas to pass the bill and get it out of the way. Of course all that was just nonsense.
The only sympathy I have for the Minister of Transport is in respect of the excessive ill usage to which he was subjected by his colleagues in the government in compelling him to wait all last fall before bringing this important measure before us. He had to give way to the Minister of National Health and Welfare who had a bill that will not become
January 27, 1967

effective until 1968. That is the only sympathy I have for the minister. I thought it was ridiculous of him just before Christmas-I have referred to Hansard to see what he said at that time-to suggest to us that by sitting all night or another day before Chrismas we might pass the bill and then we might get certain advantages. He is gradually learning by experience. I think he has learned the lesson that a bill of this magnitude requires careful study by the house. That careful study has been given.
One thing in which the opposition may take some pride is the fact that we prevented the minister and the government from instituting an investigation of the Crowsnest pass rates and leaving the impression abroad that there is something wrong with those rates. The two methods which the minister devised were rejected by this house, one the mandatory instruction to the commission to investigate the rates and the other the indirect permission to the railways to make application to the commission, when it would become mandatory for the commission to investigate them. That was thrown out by the combined efforts of the opposition in this chamber.
I do not doubt for one minute that the government may institute an inquiry into those rates if they are foolish enough to do it. But it has to be by way of governmental responsibility, and that is just where I want the responsibility placed. Let the Liberal government institute that inquiry, and the people of western Canada will know what answer to give them. The opposition performed a valuable service to western Canada by the action it took.
No bill in my experience has pursued a more tortuous route than this one. It was introduced and then withdrawn. It was reintroduced in September and referred to a committee. It was amended 60 or 70 times in that committee. I have the greatest sympathy for the legal draftsmen who prepare bills for this house. I understand something of the nature of that difficult work. They must have been driven frantic by the instructions received from this minister. A bill that has to be amended to that extent at the committee stage must have been very badly conceived in the beginning.
Not content with that amendment in the committee, we had amendment after amendment in committee of the whole house. No bill has suffered more amendment in the course of its progress through the house than this one. No bill has had more words expressed 23033-7811
Transportation
about it by the minister piloting it through the house than this one. If there is a page in Hansard dealing with this bill on which the minister did not make himself heard, it is an exception. This will stand as a record for all time, and I hope as a guide to other ministers to take a different course of action. But this minister is verbose, has to be very active and likes to wear himself out in the process. Of course we assisted him in so doing.
He may now rest on his laurels, but I do not want him to be carried away and think he has accomplished something that is simply wonderful, because I think it is a very bad example of how to put legislation through the House of Commons and I hope nobody else will imitate it.

There are those who argue that everything should be done in two or three days, but when we are dealing with a bill of this nature and size, one which will affect virtually everyone in Canada and deals with the transportation system, which is vital to our existence, we are fully justified in taking the time that we have on this bill, with the sole exception of some of the repetitious remarks made by the minister.
Yesterday the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) had some strong words to say with regard to the news media of this country. I think those remarks were justified and I say this for the foEowing reason. About two and a half years ago the members of the press gallery conducted an informal poU and asked their members to answer the foEowing question:	"Which member of the House of
Commons could be most easEy spared?" I was the winner of that poE although I thought it would have been won by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). However, I won it easily. Last fall it appeared to me that the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) was creeping up to take over my position, and yesterday when I heard the hon. member for Acadia I was a Ettle alarmed because I thought that here was another member trying to squeeze me out of my position. Therefore I agree with what the hon. member for Acadia said for the benefit of my friends in the press gaEery and I think they might very well read his words.

I would not use some of the expressions that he used but he was trying to draw to their attention and that of other people in this country that parEament as an institution performs a function which is essential to Canada, and although it may seem to the outside observer that the work we do is rather slow and ponderous the fact is that it is essential and that it is carried out with the freedom of speech which is so desirable. I am prepared to grant that now and again some time is wasted. But the essential work of the country is being done here through the means of the freedom of speech which prevails in this chamber. Nothing can be concealed that we can stir up and discover. Statements that are distorted can be corrected. Unfortunately this is not the situation with regard to some other things in our society. We have been performing here faithful, honest and hard work, and although this session has lasted now for 195 days I chaEenge anyone to say and be believed that we have been spending our time wrangling and indulging in ineffective debate. The minister and I can exchange a few humorous remarks without becoming bad friends. He has my respect.
I do not like all the things that the minister does, but we have been doing honest and hard work which should be recognized in this country. As the hon. member for Acadia said yesterday, the news media failed to give their attention to what has been going on in this chamber during the last two weeks with regard to a major change in the method of dealing with transportation, a change which will vitally affect everyone in this country. So far as the news media are concerned, we have seen and heard nothing but skimpy reports of this debate.
With those remarks I uphold parEament as an institution and I strive to maintain my position in the informal Gallup poE that may be taken in the future in the press gaEery.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) for having complied so graciously with the request we made yesterday and for having tabled today the correspondence exchanged between the Quebec government and the federal government on transport problems, and more specifically the imphcations of BiE No. C-231.
On consulting the various letters exchanged, we note that certain passages are most revealing. For instance, in the first letter sent to aE the premiers, dated August 4, 1966,
January 27, 1967

the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) said, as shown on page 2 of his letter:
-it would be desirable for discussions to be held between officials of the federal and provincial governments in an exploratory fashion.
In the previous paragraphs of his letter, the Prime Minister referred to highway safety problems, and to the possibility of standardizing highway and interprovincial regulations.
[DOT] (1.10 p.m.)
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that the date on this letter which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) drafted and sent to the provincial premiers was August 4, 1966. In his letter, he of course expresses the hope that federal and provincial government officials hold discussions with respect to these problems. Now, when we look at the time the federal government chose to introduce its resolution in this regard, we find that it was during the month of August, and the bill itself was introduced on August 29. What immediately comes to mind is the fact that, while the right hon. Prime Minister proposes that discussions be held with respect to the problems arising from any piece of legislation, at the same time, without waiting for these discussions to be held, he puts a resolution before the house, and introduces the bill itself on August 29.
An answer from the Quebec premier, Hon. Daniel Johnson, dated October 13, raises important considerations and I quote:
I shall not try to hide from you that, whatever may be the promises of future consultation, the government of Quebec looks most unfavourably upon the fact that the federal government wishes to acquire the right to exempt an undertaking from the jurisdiction of the provincial boards so as to place it under the authority of the future Canadian Transport Commission. Already, in 1954, Quebec had objected to the discretionary powers the federal government reserved itself under section 5 of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act: in our opinion, this was holding back with one hand what one was giving with the other. It seems now that our opinion was well founded. Indeed, the whole arrangement of 1954 is presently being questioned again.
And, Hon. Daniel Johnson, in his letter of October 13, continues with these words:
In fact, I was very surprised by the haste in which this measure concerning motor vehicle transport was submitted to parliament. Your letter dated August 4th, 1966 emphasizes the necessity of holding federal-provincial discussions so as to determine how we can best settle the problems that face us in this field. I wonder how such discussions could possibly be useful now that the federal government has already decided beforehand what would be their conclusions. If your government sincerely favours provincial consultation, it should necessarily proceed to such consultation before making its decisions, not after. The
Transportation
presentation of such a measure as the one provided for in Part III of Bill C-231 might eventually be the result of our discussions but it could certainly never be the preliminaries to them. For this is putting the cart before the horse.
Therefore, the government of Quebec asks you, as a token of good faith, to strike out of Bill C-231 Part III dealing with extra-provincial motor vehicle transport so that the discussions you proposed in your letter of August 4th. 1966, may take place in normal conditions. For. in such a critical field as this, it is only by holding discussions in the best of circumstances that one may hope to reach solutions satisfactory to the legitimate interests of every government and the common good of all citizens.
Mr. Speaker, from the letter of October 13, we see that the Quebec premier rightly accuses the government of the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada of putting the cart before the horse, by inviting on August 4 the provincial representatives to meet the federal officials in order to discuss and set up jointly standards for the field of transport. Then, before the provinces had had time to answer, the federal government, putting the cart before the horse, moved the resolution in the house and the bill, nicely cooked up, completely ready, was introduced on August 29.
We note, in his letter of October 13, the Quebec premier's well-advised comments on this way of going about it. On October 20, 1966, the right hon. Prime Minister replied to the October 13 letter of Hon. Daniel Johnson.
Among other things, he said this:
It was in accordance with this exclusive federal jurisdiction that the federal parliament took action to confer upon provincial agencies the authority to act as agents of the federal government in regard to movements of this sort-
In this paragraph, as well as in the previous paragraphs, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister refers to the federal legislation which had been introducted and passed in 1954 and which left with the provincial agencies, the authority to legislate and to regulate in the field of motor vehicle transport.
And, in another letter that the Quebec premier wrote to the right hon. Prime Minister, on November 15, 1966, the following considerations are removed, and to do that, Hon. Daniel Johnson says this:
-expressed very serious doubts regarding the use of such meetings, if the latter take place, after the federal government's decisions have all been made irreversibly. It would seem, judging by your answer, that such is the case.
Indeed, after reading your letter of October 20 concerning Part III of Bill C-231 regarding the national transport policy, I understand that your government does not intend to comply with the

request I made in my letter dated October 13, 1966, asking you to delete, as a token of good faith, this part of the bill.
Under the circumstances, I do not see to what purpose officials of our two governments could meet to discuss cooperation. Your government seems determined to follow the policy it has established in this field as in others, regardless of the provinces' views. What good could there be in holding repeated meetings that would lead nowhere?
Those, Mr. Speaker, were the views exchanged between the Quebec government and the federal government. I had a hunch, even before I could read that correspondence, that things had been handled here, in Ottawa, in the usual way.
A few years ago the federal government was wont to refer to the friendly and open relations that should exist between the federal and provincial governments, and that procedure was called co-operative federalism.
Well, with regard to several pieces of legislation, the central government took unilateral action so often that the spokesmen of the Liberal government in Ottawa no longer dare use the expression co-operative federalism, either in this house or at official dinners, because they have never put it into practice. No matter how well that expression sounds, its application proved awkward and inefficient, precisely because of the dishonesty of the federal Liberal government.
It is being asked not to deal unilaterally with many administrative problems in Canada, either on the fiscal, political and administrative levels, or with regard to social security.
Neither the central government nor the ten provincial governments should live as bees, each in its own hive. There should be cooperation between intelligent human beings, between men of good faith. It is apparent once again in the case of this bill that the federal government had made all the decisions, that everything was cooked up-the resolution and the bill-at the very moment the letter was being sent, pro forma, to the provinces, seeking their co-operation, consultations with them and close understanding. Everything had been prepared and cooked up and the bills introduced almost at the same time as the prime minister's letter to the provinces was being written.
Well such is the process that increases tensions in Canada, first between Canadians and between the provincial governments and the central government.
[DOT] (1.20 p.m.)
It is the wrong way to do it. I call it autocratic federalism. The central government decides by itself unilaterally puts the

provinces before a decision it has taken alone and, after it has got its bearings and is firmly in control, only then does it ask for their co-operation. It is ridiculous, it is even insulting for the provinces, because when dealing with them the central government does not consider the provincial governments as sovereign and independent governments in their field, in a spirit of true federalism, but rather acts like a father who looks condescendingly at his little girls, alone, immature, under age, and takes all the decisions alone, just like parents who decide for their children who are still under age or too young to have judgment and intelligence. The father does not consult children of seven or eight, or four or five; he decides everything and then tells the children what he has decided.
That is what the federal government does and unfortunately that attitude has become widespread in the last few years here in Ottawa. It emphasizes tension and misunderstanding between the provinces and the central government, and particularly between the Quebec government and the central government's relations with the rest of Canada.
When I talk about the Quebec government, I am not referring to any political party, I mean the successive Quebec governments. It was the same thing when a Liberal government was in power in Quebec and right now it is the same with the Union Nationale government.
I submit, sir, that there must be an end to these hypocritical, insulting and injurious practices in the relations between the central government and the provincial authorities.
I do not intend to take up the constitutional aspects of the issue again today; these were dealt with at length on September 6, 1966, as may be seen on pages 8074 and following of Hansard.
This correspondence does not bring out the constitutional aspect so much as it reveals the attitude of the central government in the matter. We understand, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian constitution, supported by certain Privy Council rulings, has granted jurisdiction to the central government in the field of interprovincial, extraprovincial and international transport. The constitution itself and rulings such as the one handed down by the Privy Council in the Winert case in 1954, acknowledge this jurisdiction. It is not so much the costitutional aspects as the way of dealing with the matter, in practice, that comes out in the correspondence between the

right hon. Prime Minister and the premier of Quebec.
Now, we know that, in fact, for a hundred years now, the central government has left to the provinces legislation and regulation in the field of motor vehicle transport. Indeed, a federal act passed in 1954 even recognized the practice. This act entitled Motor Vehicle Transport Act confirmed this; sections 3 and 4 sanctioned the agreements whereby the central government left to the provinces legislation and regulation in that field.
Today, through Bill No. C-231, the central government wishes to recover its constitutional authority. That is clear to me. But what a way to go about it, Mr. Speaker. The province of Quebec has legislated, has instituted a system of rules and regulations, and now the federal government wishes to retrieve, with a view of placing them under the Canadian Transport Commission, the modes of transport by air, water, truck and pipeline as well as by motor vehicle.
The central government has a right to have such a philosophy, but its approach to the problem is to be rejected. After letting the provinces, including Quebec, legislate and regulate on the matter for so many years, the federal government, before bringing in such legislation, should have had discussions, and consultations, in the precise spirit of the letter that the right hon. Prime Minister wrote on August 4. Instead of making such meetings possible, of discussing for the very purpose of making this return, this recovery, possible and instead of negotiating certain areas on which the provinces have a right to continue to legislate, such as the issue of licenses, traffic control, in a word, several areas of the trucking field, the central government, by the way it proceeded, had its legislation all concocted at the time they wrote a letter, as a matter of form, to the premiers of the provinces.
Such a procedure is insulting, harmful, and does not contribute anything toward solving the problem uniformly or restoring proper balance in the trucking industry across Canada. Furthermore, the procedure is wrong and protests recently lodged by the Quebec government and the Quebec leader of the opposition are warranted; as a matter of fact, I think they should be repeated here in this house to show the government and the minister that it is not good procedure to put the cart before the horse.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has just made a point that cannot in any way be reconciled with the argument I was developing. Of course, the minister is repeating the same assurances that were given in the correspondence with the premier of the province of Quebec. Well, all the assurances given by this government are such that they are likely to cause concern to the Quebec government.
And how funny it was yesterday, in this house, to hear the Minister of Transport state, with the zest for which he is famous, that no member in this house was more mindful than he of the respect of the letter and spirit of the Canadian constitution. I found that statement extremely amusing, Mr. Speaker. And it is certainly not the kind of statement which the minister made yesterday and seems willing to repeat today which will dissolve all our fears about the letter and the spirit of the Canadian constitution which the minister and the present government are claiming to respect. As a matter of fact, that commitment is not borne out by the facts in this session or particularly during the last two years the present Liberal government has been in office. Mr. Speaker, the minister has assured us during this session that no other hon. member has more respect than he has for the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution, but he is a member of a government which has presented to us bills which are absolutely contrary to the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution.

January 27, 1967

I am referring for instance to medicare, to the increase in old age pensions and the rest. In the field of mining, for instance, on the continental shelf, all sorts of tricks and means are being used, though natural resources clearly and explicitly belong to the provinces to take them away from provincial jurisdiction. In fact, the provinces are being hamstrung by dragging the question before a court which is not empowered to rule on constitutional matters in Canada.
They also have, in the course of the present session, through the establishment of a cultural centre, infringed upon the field of culture and education which is under the jurisdiction of the provinces according to the letter and the spirit of the Canadian constitution.
Here is a government and an hon. minister who have co-operated during this very session in scuttling and despoiling the spirit and the letter of the Canadian constitution. When the hon. minister rises, as he did yesterday and today and, with talent and charm I must say-because he is very charming- gives the hon. members in this house and specially the province of Quebec, the assurance that there are no grounds for anxiety, well then, I say that if we consider some legislation which this government has introduced during this and other sessions, for instance on school allowances, on student loans and also that political program of handing out scholarships to students, this is spoliation of the Canadian constitution, both in letter and in spirit. The assurance given by this government cannot dispel our anxiety in the province of Quebec as far as observance of the constitution.
And as to the provisions of the Canadian constitution that must be observed, in the field of transport, it is not so much the constitutional aspect as the method of the present government in putting the cart before the horses that we are discussing. It is the method that needs to be pointed out and criticized, for it is to be blamed for trying to face the provinces with the fait accompli while, for diplomatic reasons, they had been invited at the same time to meet the provinces to discuss and arrive at decisions knowing full well that all decisions had been arrived at and that the resolution and the bill had already been drafted and cooked up. This way of doing things, I feel, is unacceptable in the field of a well balanced relationship, in good faith and equality, each in his own area, between the

central government and the provincial governments.
I understand quite well the stand taken by the Minister of Transport who says that the federal government has jurisdiction under the constitution and judgments of the Privy Council. This is all very well, but before preparing his bill, he should have discussed the withdrawal and extension of the right to legislate of the provinces in certain fields of highway transport. It is just like in civil law, Mr. Speaker. Let us imagine that the minister, probably to play a trick on me, steals my car and puts it in his yard. I have no right then to go on his property with my friends to retrieve my car, because this would be a trespass under criminal law. In short, the car actually belongs to me, since I have the ownership and registration papers, but I cannot go on his property to retrieve it. What I must do, Mr. Speaker, as you know very well, is to send a summons preceding a seizure under a prior claim. The provisions of civil law are based on the honesty and intelligence of man, of the human being, from his adolescence. The basis of the law is the common sense and the sense of justice of human beings. That is how the federal government should proceed.
If it wants to take over the jurisdiction allotted to it by the constitution with regard to interprovincial, extraprovincial and international transport, I am not against it. I respect the constitutional powers of the central government as much as those of the provinces, but I object to this off-hand and insulting procedure. If it had only met with provincial representatives, especially those of the province of Quebec, in order to discuss and prepare this legislation, we would not be faced today with the situation whereby the Quebec government is asking for the removal of Part III of a bill prepared without consultation and discussion. The Quebec government is asking the minister to defer, to remove Part III from this bill, that is, from clause 28 to clause 36, precisely because in certain fields, the Quebec government has enacted regulations and passed pieces of legislation on which persons of good faith ought to agree.
Before taking over, in what I call an offhand manner, that constitutional authority, the minister should have given a formal notice. The funny part of it is that the Prime Minister gave such a notice in his first letter of August 4 to the provinces, asking them to meet in order to discuss all those problems.

But before sending that notice, he had already prepared his resolution and his bill without giving the provinces an opportunity to discuss the matter.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
Thus, this is absolutely superficial and did nothing but emphasize the tensions between the Quebec government and the central government, when it would be so easy during this centennial year to show less arrogance, less inclination to act unilaterally to get the Canadians, the governments closer together and to give Canadian federalism a real sense of balance, understanding and respect for one another, in short to act with more tact and intelligence.
I am not sure of it, because the letters do not mention it, but I think that the members of the Quebec legislature, even some Canadians, are worried also about that administrative monster which is being created through this Canadian Transport Commission which will in fact regulate the whole field of transportation in Canada.
Whether in the fields of air, sea and road transportation, it is giving much power to a transportation commission set up by the federal government because it will regulate means of transport including the trucking industry in Canada and in Quebec whereas the C.N.R. which operates a trucking service comes under the same creating body, the central government. This, Mr. Speaker, leads us to wonder if that national commission, that administrative monster, will be able directly or indirectly to administer with true objectivity the field of transportation in Canada.
It would have been important among other things, for the federal government to discuss those matters before presenting a bill already drafted.
Those are the various points I wanted to submit once again to the minister. I do not know whether I have convinced him. He shakes his head negatively. Obviously, he does not understand easily.
Mr. Speaker, I felt I had to report on these provisions contained in the correspondence between the Quebec government and the federal government, and even if the hon. minister cannot understand, even if he refuses to change his attitude, I think the time will come very soon when circumstances will force him and some of his colleagues to treat 23033-782
